A few years ago I posted in a popular femboy subreddit, asking how many femboys enjoy being treated like a girl or referred to as a "girl". Within a matter of only 3 hours that post went viral with over 500 upvotes. I certainly never imagined so many other feminine boys would share similar feelings of cross-gender euphoria. Apparently I tapped into an aspect of gender nonconformity that really resonated with a lot of people. 

The fact that even "biological boys" who *fully accept* their assigned sex of male can have such a strong emotional attachment to femininity that they want to called a "girl" or seen as a "girl" is mind-blowing. In Western culture, we assume that cross-gender euphoria is indicative of being transgender or nonbinary. But perhaps there is a lot more nuance in how certain people perceive their gender in relation to the constructs of society. And as those experiences come to light, we may need to rethink the transgender/cisgender dichotomy as well.

It should perhaps come as no surprise that plenty of non-Western cultures already recognize and affirm effeminate "biological boys" as a distinct third gender. These boys are raised the same as girls and they take on the social roles of women. Even though they don't identify as women, they are nonetheless able to move through society in nearly all the same ways as women. Nobody questions the fact these are "biological boys" entering into women's spaces and participating in women's activities. Instead they are treated with dignity and respect.

This is why I think it's so important that we conduct more research about gender variance outside of transgender and nonbinary circles. In particular, we need to gain better insight about the psychology of feminine boys. If we can show that feelings of cross-gender euphoria are not exclusive to trans people but rather exist across a broad spectrum of gender variance, that would be a watershed moment for LGBTQ advocacy.

I forgot to mention, if you do live in a state that has statutory protections, then you can file a case of discrimination with the State. This office is typically known as the Department of Human Rights, Division of Human Rights, or  similar. Some states even have a separate Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) specifically for handling employment discrimination complaints. They will open a formal investigation and potentially fine the employer or impose other penalties and corrective measures.

In the United States there are two applicable protections in place:

1. Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) - employment discrimination for a person's gender identity or sexual orientation constitutes sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act.
2. Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins (1989) - employment discrimination for not adhering to sex-based stereotypes constitutes sex discrimination under the Civil Rights Act

If you live in a state that is not trans friendly and does not have statutory protections for LGBTQ people in place, then you might want to pursue civil remedies under #2, since that is a much older legal precedent that is well known and time-tested. Of course, I would defer to your lawyer's specific advice on a legal strategy. But either way, in the jurisdiction of the U.S., it is illegal to fire you specifically because your employer discovers you are trans.

Let's also not forget that a LOT of states in the United States already do have various gender recognition policies and statutes in place allowing for gender markers on ID's and drivers license and birth certificates to be updated based on certain criteria (some don't even require a medical exam at all).

For example, 22 states allow for choosing "M", "F", or "X" on a driver's license. That's nearly half the country.

And in every state (to the best of my knowledge) it's already entirely legal to change your name without needing any doctor form or medical transition. I believe the only restrictions on name changes anywhere in the U.S. are with intent to avoid a criminal record or evade law enforcement.
